The bronzy inca (Coeligena coeligena) is a medium-sized hummingbird inhabiting the humid Andean cloud forests from Colombia to Bolivia. Recently hatched chicks emerge from their eggs at a remarkably small size, with an initial wet weight of only 0.88 grams [Ww0 = 0.88 grams], a value that reflects the species' altricial developmental mode. Field observations indicate that incubation lasts approximately 15.5 days [ab = approximately 15.5 days] at an average nest temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], a thermal condition that accelerates embryonic development relative to cooler montane environments where incubation may be prolonged. This modest hatchling mass, representing roughly one-seventh of the eventual adult female body mass, places the young bird in a phase of intense parental dependency, during which the nestling must nearly double its weight on a daily basis to achieve the adult body size required for independent foraging.

Adult body mass in Coeligena coeligena exhibits moderate but consistent sexual dimorphism, with females reaching an ultimate wet weight of 6.2 grams [Wwi = 6.2 grams] while males attain a slightly larger ultimate wet weight of 6.7 grams [Wwi = 6.7 grams]. This difference, amounting to approximately eight percent of total body mass, is typical among hummingbird species where males often possess a more robust flight apparatus to support territorial defense and courtship displays. Field surveys across multiple elevations from 1,500 to 2,800 meters have confirmed that both sexes maintain these mass ranges across their distribution, with only minor seasonal fluctuations linked to the availability of nectar resources during the dry and wet seasons. The smaller body size of females presumably reduces the energetic demand of egg production and incubation, though metabolic costs remain substantial for a bird of this mass when hovering at high altitudes.

Under the thermally regulated conditions of an active hummingbird, typically around 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C], the developmental trajectory of the bronzy inca follows a precise schedule. Fledging, defined as the achievement of sustained flight and departure from the nest, occurs approximately 23 days after hatching [tx = approximately 23 days after hatching], a period during which the wing feathers fully emerge and the juvenile achieves approximately eighty percent at a temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C] of adult mass. This fledging interval, ranging between 22 and 24 days in most documented broods, is consistent with the duration reported for other medium-sized Andean hummingbirds. Following fledging, the young bird enters a juvenile phase characterized by continued growth, refinement of foraging skills, and gradual reduction of parental provisioning, which ceases entirely several weeks after nest departure as the individual becomes nutritionally independent.

Sexual maturation in the bronzy inca is attained relatively early compared to other Andean birds of similar body size, with puberty reached at 69 days after hatching [tp = 69 days after hatching] when the bird is maintained at 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. At this time, gonadal development is complete and the individual is physiologically capable of reproduction, though actual breeding is typically deferred until social and ecological conditions are favorable. The onset of first reproduction occurs 365 days after birth [tR = 365 days after birth] under the same standard thermal conditions of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C], a timing that aligns the nesting cycle with the peak flowering period of the high-altitude plant community. Females then produce a single clutch annually [F_R_i = single clutch annually], each containing precisely 2 eggs [N_R_i = each containing precisely 2 eggs], a constrained reproductive output that is typical for hummingbirds and reflects the high energetic cost of egg production and the extended period of parental care required for each brood.

Lifespan data for the bronzy inca, derived from mark-recapture studies in the Peruvian Andes, indicate that the maximum longevity recorded in the wild is approximately 7.7 years [am = approximately 7.7 years] for individuals living under average body temperatures of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C], a value that suggests a relatively rapid life-history pace compared to larger Neotropical birds. Basal metabolic rate measurements from respirometry trials conducted in the field reveal a resting oxygen consumption of 34.55 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 34.55 milliliters of oxygen per hour] at 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C], representing the maximum basal metabolic rate recorded for this species. This elevated metabolic demand, characteristic of all hummingbirds, is sustained almost entirely by nectar intake, and the bird must consume more than its own body mass in floral nectar daily to meet the energy requirements imposed by hovering flight and high-altitude living.
